primitives.name: UnitOfWork
primitives.purpose: Tracks object changes during a business transaction and flushes them to storage as one atomic commit or rollback.
primitives.api_signature:
from typing import Protocol, Any

class UnitOfWork(Protocol):
    def register_new(self, obj: Any) -> None: ...
    def register_dirty(self, obj: Any) -> None: ...
    def register_removed(self, obj: Any) -> None: ...
    def commit(self) -> None: ...
    def rollback(self) -> None: ...
    def __enter__(self) -> 'UnitOfWork': ...
    def __exit__(self, exc_type, exc, tb) -> bool: ...
invariants: A successful commit MUST apply every registered new, dirty, and removed object in a single database transaction.
On any exception before commit, the implementation MUST rollback and discard all tracked changes.
The same object instance SHALL NEVER be registered in more than one of (new, dirty, removed) within one unit.
A UnitOfWork instance CANNOT be reused after commit or rollback; a fresh unit MUST be opened for the next transaction.
Repositories operating inside a unit MUST enlist their mutations with that unit rather than writing directly to the database.
The unit ALWAYS exposes its lifecycle via context-manager semantics so leaks on exception paths are impossible.
primitives.extension_contract: Downstream tools extend UnitOfWork by subclassing the abstract implementation or by registering a new flush phase hook (before_commit, on_commit, after_commit) via a register callable; the existing order of inserts, updates, deletes MUST remain intact.
primitives.consumption_example:
def transfer(uow: UnitOfWork, src_id: int, dst_id: int, amount: int) -> None:
    with uow:
        src = accounts.get(src_id)
        dst = accounts.get(dst_id)
        src.debit(amount)
        dst.credit(amount)
        uow.register_dirty(src)
        uow.register_dirty(dst)
        uow.commit()

sources.locator: Chapter 11, Unit of Work pattern, pp. 184-194
Chapter 12, Repositories, Unit of Work collaboration, pp. 416-419

primitives.why_essential: Without one shared primitive, each tool invents its own commit boundary and transactions leak across features, producing partial writes and lost updates when two tools share a request.
alternatives_considered: Auto-commit per repository call: trades atomicity for simplicity and breaks multi-aggregate invariants.
Session-per-request middleware only: implicit boundaries hide rollback semantics from the caller.
Manual BEGIN/COMMIT in each tool: duplicates logic and diverges on error handling.

primitives.name: Repository
primitives.purpose: Mediates between the domain model and data mapping layer using a collection-like interface to access aggregate roots.
primitives.api_signature:
from typing import Protocol, Generic, TypeVar, Optional, Iterable

T = TypeVar('T')

class Repository(Protocol, Generic[T]):
    def get(self, id: object) -> Optional[T]: ...
    def add(self, entity: T) -> None: ...
    def remove(self, entity: T) -> None: ...
    def find(self, spec: object) -> Iterable[T]: ...
invariants: A Repository MUST only expose aggregate roots, NEVER internal child entities of another aggregate.
Query methods MUST accept a Specification object or a named finder and SHALL NOT leak SQL, ORM, or storage syntax to callers.
A single logical aggregate type MUST have exactly one Repository; duplicate repositories for the same root are FORBIDDEN.
Mutations (add, remove) MUST enlist with the active UnitOfWork and NEVER issue direct writes bypassing it.
The Repository CANNOT return stale in-memory copies when an IdentityMap is present; it MUST consult the map first.
primitives.extension_contract: Domain tools extend Repository by subclassing the abstract base per aggregate root, or by registering a new Specification translator via a decorator; the collection-contract (get/add/remove/find) SHALL remain invariant under extension.
primitives.why_essential: Without a shared contract, each tool reinvents query surfaces; domain logic ends up coupled to ORM internals and test doubles diverge in behavior across tools.
alternatives_considered: Active Record per entity: couples persistence with domain behavior; breaks aggregate boundaries at scale.
Raw DAO returning rows: leaks storage shape into the domain layer.
Query objects without a collection facade: loses the get/add/remove symmetry Evans requires.

primitives.name: IdentityMap
primitives.purpose: Caches loaded domain objects by identity inside one session so the same row is never represented twice in memory.
primitives.api_signature:
from typing import Protocol, Any, Optional

class IdentityMap(Protocol):
    def get(self, type_: type, id: object) -> Optional[Any]: ...
    def add(self, obj: Any) -> None: ...
    def remove(self, type_: type, id: object) -> None: ...
    def contains(self, type_: type, id: object) -> bool: ...
invariants: Given the same (type, id) within one session, the IdentityMap MUST return the same Python object reference on every lookup.
An object CANNOT be inserted twice for the same identity; a second add with a new instance SHALL raise a conflict error.
The map MUST be scoped to a single UnitOfWork or session and NEVER shared across concurrent transactions.
On UnitOfWork disposal the map ALWAYS clears its contents; retaining references beyond the session is FORBIDDEN.
primitives.extension_contract: Storage backends extend IdentityMap by implementing the Protocol and binding it into the UnitOfWork factory; eviction policies are added via a register hook, but referential-identity within a session SHALL NOT be weakened.
primitives.consumption_example:
def load_order(repo, imap: IdentityMap, order_id: int):
    cached = imap.get(Order, order_id)
    if cached is not None:
        return cached
    order = repo.get(order_id)
    imap.add(order)
    return order
primitives.why_essential: Absent a shared map, two reads of the same row yield two divergent objects; updates on one silently overwrite the other when flushed through the same UnitOfWork.
alternatives_considered: Per-query result caching: does not guarantee referential identity across queries.
Rely on ORM internal session cache only: obscures the contract and blocks non-ORM repositories.
Global process cache: violates session scoping and corrupts concurrent transactions.

primitives.name: DataMapper
primitives.purpose: Moves state between in-memory domain objects and rows in storage while keeping both ignorant of each other.
primitives.api_signature:
from typing import Protocol, TypeVar, Generic, Any

T = TypeVar('T')

class DataMapper(Protocol, Generic[T]):
    def load(self, row: dict) -> T: ...
    def insert(self, entity: T) -> dict: ...
    def update(self, entity: T) -> dict: ...
    def delete(self, entity: T) -> dict: ...
invariants: The domain object MUST have no import-time or runtime dependency on storage types; persistence knowledge SHALL live exclusively in the mapper.
Given a row r, load(r) followed by insert or update on the resulting entity MUST yield a row with the same identity key.
The mapper CANNOT mutate the domain object for persistence convenience; derived columns MUST be computed in map methods, never injected into the domain.
A DataMapper NEVER issues database I/O directly; it returns parameterized payloads the UnitOfWork flush executes.
primitives.extension_contract: New persistent types extend DataMapper by implementing the Protocol per aggregate and registering the pair via a register call on the mapper registry; storage-specific encodings plug in through an adapter (for JSONB, arrays, encrypted columns) without the domain being recompiled.
primitives.why_essential: Without a shared mapper contract, every tool either smears ORM-specific types across the domain or reinvents row-to-object translation with subtle conversion bugs.
alternatives_considered: Active Record: collapses domain and persistence and prevents pure-domain unit tests.
Table Module with record sets: suits simple CRUD but not rich aggregates.
ORM auto-mapping only: magical, brittle across schema evolution, and ties the domain to ORM types.

primitives.name: Specification
primitives.purpose: Encapsulates a predicate over a domain object so selection, validation, and building criteria share one reusable rule.
primitives.api_signature:
from typing import Protocol, TypeVar, Generic

T = TypeVar('T')

class Specification(Protocol, Generic[T]):
    def is_satisfied_by(self, candidate: T) -> bool: ...
    def and_(self, other: 'Specification[T]') -> 'Specification[T]': ...
    def or_(self, other: 'Specification[T]') -> 'Specification[T]': ...
    def not_(self) -> 'Specification[T]': ...
invariants: is_satisfied_by MUST be a pure predicate: no I/O, no mutation of the candidate, and NEVER time-dependent unless time is injected.
Composed specifications (and_, or_, not_) MUST preserve the identity laws of boolean algebra so refactors cannot change semantics.
A Specification CANNOT depend on the persistence layer; repository translation MUST be delegated to a separate visitor or translator.
The same Specification used for in-memory filtering and repository querying SHALL produce logically equivalent results.
primitives.extension_contract: New rules extend Specification by subclassing and overriding is_satisfied_by, or by registering a translator adapter that converts the spec tree to a backend query; composition operators SHALL NOT be overridden by subclasses.
primitives.why_essential: If selection rules live only as inline lambdas or ORM filters, the same policy gets re-implemented divergently in validation, UI filtering, and reports, making policy drift silent.
alternatives_considered: Inline lambdas per callsite: duplicated logic and no composition algebra.
Raw SQL fragments: storage-coupled and untestable in-memory.
Rule-engine DSL: heavier than needed for the 80% case and opaque to domain experts.

primitives.name: Aggregate
primitives.purpose: Defines a consistency boundary around a cluster of entities and value objects governed by a single root responsible for invariants.
invariants: Only the aggregate root MUST be referenced from outside the aggregate; external references to internal children are FORBIDDEN.
A single transaction MUST modify at most one aggregate instance; cross-aggregate changes SHALL be coordinated via domain events.
All invariants defined by the root MUST hold at the end of every public method; intermediate illegal states CANNOT be exposed.
The aggregate version NEVER decreases and MUST increment on every state-changing operation for optimistic concurrency.
External collaborators SHALL reference other aggregates by identifier only, NEVER by object reference.
primitives.extension_contract: New aggregate types extend Aggregate by subclassing the abstract root and binding repository, mapper, and event publisher via compose; invariant-enforcing methods extend by adding domain-specific commands that continue to pull events through pull_events.
primitives.why_essential: Without one shared definition, teams disagree on what constitutes a transactional boundary, and eventually consistent updates across aggregates get treated as strongly consistent, producing silent corruption.
alternatives_considered: Transaction-per-operation anemic domain: loses invariant enforcement and pushes rules into services.
Whole-graph aggregates: contention hot-spots and oversized transactions.
Entity-only modeling without roots: ambiguous ownership of invariants.

primitives.name: ValueObject
primitives.purpose: Represents a descriptive concept whose identity is defined entirely by its attributes and which is immutable once constructed.
primitives.api_signature:
from typing import Protocol

class ValueObject(Protocol):
    def __eq__(self, other: object) -> bool: ...
    def __hash__(self) -> int: ...
    def with_changes(self, **kwargs) -> 'ValueObject': ...
invariants: Instances MUST be immutable after construction; attribute assignment post-init is FORBIDDEN.
Two instances with the same attribute values MUST compare equal and MUST share the same hash.
A ValueObject CANNOT hold a reference to an Aggregate root or Entity whose identity is unstable.
Construction SHALL validate every invariant eagerly; a partially-valid instance NEVER exists.
primitives.extension_contract: Domain tools extend ValueObject by subclassing a frozen dataclass base and registering a coercion adapter for serialization; adding derived fields is allowed through with_changes, but mutation in place SHALL remain FORBIDDEN.
primitives.consumption_example:
def apply_discount(price: ValueObject, pct: int) -> ValueObject:
    return price.with_changes(amount=price.amount * (100 - pct) // 100)
primitives.why_essential: Without a shared contract, Money, Email, DateRange are each reimplemented per tool with divergent validation, and equality semantics silently diverge between comparisons and hashing.
alternatives_considered: Plain dicts or tuples: lose validation and type safety.
Mutable dataclasses: break equality-by-value and invite aliasing bugs.
Primitive obsession: scatters validation across every consumer.

primitives.name: BoundedContext
primitives.purpose: Declares the explicit linguistic and model boundary within which one ubiquitous language and one set of invariants apply.
invariants: Every Aggregate type MUST be owned by exactly one BoundedContext; shared ownership across contexts is FORBIDDEN.
Cross-context calls MUST pass through an AntiCorruptionLayer or a published-language schema; raw object sharing is NEVER permitted.
The ubiquitous language of a context SHALL be locally consistent: one term CANNOT carry two meanings inside the same BoundedContext.
A BoundedContext ALWAYS exposes its integration points through a ContextMap relationship (Customer-Supplier, Conformist, Partnership, Open Host).
primitives.extension_contract: New domains are introduced by subclassing BoundedContext and registering translator adapters for each upstream or downstream neighbor; redefining an existing context's language in place is FORBIDDEN — the extension MUST declare a new context.

sources.locator: Chapter 2, Domains, Subdomains, Bounded Contexts, pp. 43-80

primitives.why_essential: Without an explicit shared primitive, model terms bleed across services, the same word means different things, and integration bugs recur because nobody owns the translation.
alternatives_considered: One canonical enterprise model: impossible to keep consistent at scale and collapses under concurrent change.
Per-service ad hoc boundaries: no shared vocabulary for integration policy.
Database-schema-as-boundary: couples physical storage to logical context.

primitives.name: AntiCorruptionLayer
primitives.purpose: Translates between a local model and a foreign or legacy model so upstream semantics cannot leak into the local BoundedContext.
primitives.api_signature:
from typing import Protocol, TypeVar

Local = TypeVar('Local')
Foreign = TypeVar('Foreign')

class AntiCorruptionLayer(Protocol):
    def to_local(self, foreign: Foreign) -> Local: ...
    def to_foreign(self, local: Local) -> Foreign: ...
    def guard(self, foreign: Foreign) -> None: ...
invariants: Foreign types MUST NEVER cross the boundary of the local BoundedContext; all inbound payloads SHALL be translated through to_local before entering domain logic.
guard MUST reject inbound payloads that violate local invariants and raise before the payload reaches any local aggregate.
Translation SHALL be stateless with respect to the local domain; the ACL CANNOT read or mutate local repositories during translation.
Versioning of the foreign contract MUST be explicit; unversioned ACLs are FORBIDDEN.
primitives.extension_contract: New integrations extend AntiCorruptionLayer by implementing an adapter per external system and registering the facade with the local BoundedContext; versioned schemas plug in via decorator over to_local / to_foreign so older payloads continue to be handled.
primitives.consumption_example:
def consume(msg, acl: AntiCorruptionLayer, repo):
    acl.guard(msg)
    local = acl.to_local(msg)
    repo.add(local)

sources.locator: Chapter 3, Context Maps, Anticorruption Layer, pp. 106-111

primitives.why_essential: Without a shared primitive, each integration tool silently imports upstream vocabulary, and legacy system concepts infect the domain model until refactors become impossible.
alternatives_considered: Direct consumer against upstream SDK: couples domain to upstream release cadence.
One central translation service: bottleneck and ownership ambiguity.
Shared kernel with upstream: violates the exact coupling the ACL exists to prevent.

primitives.name: ContextMap
primitives.purpose: Catalogs every BoundedContext and the integration relationship (Partnership, Customer-Supplier, Conformist, Open Host) between each pair.
primitives.api_signature:
from typing import Protocol, Iterable, Tuple

class ContextMap(Protocol):
    def contexts(self) -> Iterable[str]: ...
    def relationship(self, upstream: str, downstream: str) -> str: ...
    def add_relationship(self, upstream: str, downstream: str, kind: str) -> None: ...
    def integrations(self) -> Iterable[Tuple[str, str, str]]: ...
invariants: Every pairwise integration between contexts MUST be classified by one of the canonical relationship kinds; ad-hoc or blank relationships are FORBIDDEN.
The graph of contexts SHALL be acyclic for Customer-Supplier relationships; a cycle CANNOT be introduced without promotion to Partnership.
A BoundedContext CANNOT participate in an integration absent from the ContextMap; shadow integrations MUST be surfaced.
Relationship changes ALWAYS require an explicit mutation through add_relationship so history is auditable.
primitives.extension_contract: New integration kinds extend ContextMap by registering a relationship-kind plugin with translation and governance semantics; existing canonical kinds SHALL NOT be redefined by downstream consumers.
primitives.why_essential: Without a shared primitive, integration policy is tribal knowledge; ownership of translations is ambiguous and producers change contracts without notifying downstream contexts.
alternatives_considered: Architecture diagrams in Confluence: rot quickly and are not programmatically enforceable.
Service catalog with no relationship kind: records existence, not governance.
ADRs only: chronicle decisions but do not expose live topology.

primitives.name: MaterializedView
primitives.purpose: Maintains a pre-computed query result kept up to date by an incremental feed so read queries never recompute from base tables.
primitives.api_signature:
from typing import Protocol, Any, Iterable

class MaterializedView(Protocol):
    @property
    def name(self) -> str: ...
    def apply(self, event: Any) -> None: ...
    def rebuild(self, source: Iterable[Any]) -> None: ...
    def query(self, criteria: object) -> Iterable[Any]: ...
invariants: apply MUST be deterministic: given the same event stream in the same order, the view state SHALL converge to the same contents.
The view CANNOT be the system of record; rebuild MUST be able to regenerate state purely from the source feed.
Reads against the view MUST tolerate bounded staleness and NEVER claim linearizability with the base data.
Schema evolution SHALL trigger a rebuild path; silent backfill with stale rows is FORBIDDEN.
primitives.extension_contract: New projections extend MaterializedView by subclassing the Protocol and registering event-handler functions via a decorator per aggregate type; storage backends plug in through an adapter interface so the same projection can target OLTP, OLAP, or a search index.

sources.locator: Chapter 11, Stream Processing, materialized views, pp. 461-466
Chapter 7, CQRS and materialized views, pp. 253-278

primitives.why_essential: Without a shared primitive, each tool builds its own cache-or-view with divergent invalidation rules and nobody can tell which rows are stale when a customer disputes a balance.
alternatives_considered: On-demand recomputation: unbounded latency for hot reads.
Hand-rolled caches with TTL: stale forever on missed invalidations.
OLAP cube refresh nightly: too coarse for operational reads.

primitives.name: ChangeDataCapture
primitives.purpose: Publishes an ordered stream of row-level changes from a source database so downstream systems can consume mutations without dual writes.
primitives.api_signature:
from typing import Protocol, Iterator, Any

class ChangeDataCapture(Protocol):
    def subscribe(self, table: str, from_position: object) -> Iterator[Any]: ...
    def checkpoint(self, position: object) -> None: ...
    def schema(self, table: str) -> dict: ...
invariants: Every committed row change in the source MUST appear in the stream exactly once in commit order; reordering across transactions is FORBIDDEN.
Consumers MUST be able to resume from a persisted checkpoint; the stream SHALL carry a monotonically increasing position.
CDC events NEVER include uncommitted changes; dirty reads are forbidden on the downstream side.
Schema changes at the source MUST surface as schema events so consumers CANNOT silently parse new columns with the old parser.
primitives.extension_contract: New sources extend ChangeDataCapture by implementing a connector plugin that emits position-tagged change events and registering it with the stream broker; transformations are added via composed filter stages that MUST NOT reorder events within a transaction.

sources.locator: Chapter 3, Transactional messaging, CDC section, pp. 96-102

primitives.why_essential: Without a shared primitive, each tool reaches for dual writes (DB then broker) and loses either the database update or the event on failure, breaking downstream consistency.
alternatives_considered: Dual write from application code: non-atomic; either DB or broker writes fail independently.
Polling last_modified columns: misses deletes and creates read load.
Trigger-based outbox inside DB: works but constrains schema and complicates migrations.

primitives.name: DomainEvent
primitives.purpose: Records an immutable fact about something meaningful that happened in the domain and can be published to downstream consumers.
invariants: A DomainEvent MUST be immutable after publication; mutation or retroactive edit is FORBIDDEN.
event_id MUST be globally unique and stable so idempotent consumers can dedupe reliably.
The event NEVER carries commands or intents; it only states that something already happened.
version SHALL increment per aggregate and serve as the ordering key within one aggregate stream.
primitives.extension_contract: New event types extend DomainEvent by subclassing a frozen event base and registering the schema with the event registry via a register call; schema evolution adds fields through additive versions, CANNOT remove or rename fields without a new event type.

sources.locator: Chapter 8, Domain Events (later-adopted glossary, reinforced in reprints)
Chapter 5, Event-driven architecture, event structure, pp. 162-170

primitives.why_essential: Without a shared primitive, each tool invents its own payload shape and identifier strategy, breaking cross-service replay, deduplication, and audit traceability.
alternatives_considered: Integration-only messages: miss the domain semantics and couple to transport.
Bare payload dicts: no stable identity, ordering, or schema contract.
CRUD notifications: leak storage shape and lose intent.

primitives.name: TransactionalOutbox
primitives.purpose: Stores outgoing messages in the same local transaction as the state change so a relay can publish them atomically with the commit.
primitives.api_signature:
from typing import Protocol, Any, Iterable

class TransactionalOutbox(Protocol):
    def enqueue(self, destination: str, payload: Any, key: str) -> None: ...
    def pending(self, limit: int) -> Iterable[dict]: ...
    def mark_published(self, message_id: str) -> None: ...
    def mark_failed(self, message_id: str, reason: str) -> None: ...
invariants: enqueue MUST write the outbox row inside the same database transaction as the originating state change; cross-transaction writes are FORBIDDEN.
A message MUST NOT be marked published until the broker has acknowledged it.
The relay SHALL deliver at-least-once; consumers MUST therefore be idempotent, and duplicate suppression CANNOT be assumed.
Ordering per partition key ALWAYS follows transaction commit order; reordering across commits is FORBIDDEN.
primitives.extension_contract: New brokers extend TransactionalOutbox by implementing a publisher adapter and registering it with the outbox relay; storage backends for the outbox table plug in through an adapter, but atomicity with the domain transaction SHALL remain invariant.
primitives.consumption_example:
def place_order(uow, outbox: TransactionalOutbox, order):
    with uow:
        orders.add(order)
        outbox.enqueue('orders.placed', order.to_event(), key=order.id)
        uow.commit()

sources.locator: Chapter 11, Idempotence and at-least-once delivery, pp. 478-483

primitives.why_essential: Without a shared primitive, tools resort to dual writes (DB + broker) and lose messages on crash between the two, producing silent data divergence across services.
alternatives_considered: Two-phase commit (XA) across DB and broker: high latency, limited broker support, operational complexity.
Publish-then-save: loses the DB write on crash, corrupts state.
Save-then-publish: loses the message on crash, breaks downstream state.

primitives.name: InboxDeduplicator
primitives.purpose: Records processed message identifiers in the consumer's database so redelivered messages are detected and skipped exactly once.
primitives.api_signature:
from typing import Protocol

class InboxDeduplicator(Protocol):
    def seen(self, message_id: str, consumer: str) -> bool: ...
    def record(self, message_id: str, consumer: str) -> None: ...
    def purge_older_than(self, iso_timestamp: str) -> int: ...
invariants: record MUST be written in the same transaction as the consumer's side-effect; writing after the side-effect is FORBIDDEN.
Given the same (message_id, consumer), seen MUST be deterministic; the consumer CANNOT double-apply the effect.
Retention policy SHALL cover at least the broker's maximum redelivery window; premature purging is NEVER allowed.
The deduplicator NEVER silently reclassifies unseen messages as duplicates; a missing record ALWAYS means first delivery.
primitives.extension_contract: Storage backends extend InboxDeduplicator by implementing the Protocol and binding the table or key space via a register call on the inbox factory; eviction policies plug in through a hook while preserving the redelivery window guarantee.
primitives.consumption_example:
def handle(msg, inbox: InboxDeduplicator, uow, apply_effect):
    with uow:
        if inbox.seen(msg.id, 'orders_consumer'):
            return
        apply_effect(msg)
        inbox.record(msg.id, 'orders_consumer')
        uow.commit()

sources.locator: Chapter 11, Exactly-once processing via idempotent writes, pp. 476-479

primitives.why_essential: Without a shared primitive, each consumer invents its own dedupe and frequently drops the 'write in same txn' rule, resulting in duplicate side-effects on replays.
alternatives_considered: Broker-only dedupe: broker windows are short; late redelivery slips through.
Consumer-side idempotent operations only: works for upserts but not for effects like sending email.
Monotonic offset tracking: loses per-message granularity and cannot recover from poisonous messages.

primitives.name: IdempotentConsumer
primitives.purpose: Applies a message's effect at most once per logical key while tolerating at-least-once delivery from the transport.
primitives.api_signature:
from typing import Protocol, Any

class IdempotentConsumer(Protocol):
    def key_for(self, message: Any) -> str: ...
    def handle(self, message: Any) -> None: ...
    def on_duplicate(self, message: Any) -> None: ...
invariants: Two messages with the same idempotency key MUST produce the same observable system state; divergence is FORBIDDEN.
handle CANNOT perform non-compensatable side-effects without first consulting an InboxDeduplicator or equivalent.
on_duplicate MUST NEVER raise as a primary error path; duplicates are an expected steady-state condition.
The consumer SHALL publish its own outputs through a TransactionalOutbox so downstream systems can dedupe similarly.
primitives.extension_contract: New consumer types extend IdempotentConsumer by subclassing, overriding key_for and handle, and registering the consumer with the bus via register; pre- and post-processing plug in via middleware while the idempotency contract SHALL remain intact.

sources.locator: Chapter 11, Fault-tolerance of stream processing, pp. 476-479

primitives.why_essential: Without a shared contract, every consumer reimplements idempotency differently, and the one that gets it wrong quietly double-charges, double-emails, or double-ships.
alternatives_considered: Exactly-once transport: not achievable end-to-end; only 'effectively-once' under specific conditions.
Manual ad-hoc dedupe per tool: inconsistent and fragile.
Pure upsert operations: ignores effectful consumers (email, payment, webhook).

primitives.name: SagaOrchestrator
primitives.purpose: Coordinates a multi-step business transaction across services by driving each step and triggering compensations when a later step fails.
primitives.api_signature:
from typing import Protocol, Any, Iterable, Tuple

class SagaOrchestrator(Protocol):
    def start(self, correlation_id: str, input: Any) -> None: ...
    def step(self, correlation_id: str, name: str, outcome: Any) -> None: ...
    def compensate(self, correlation_id: str, from_step: str) -> None: ...
    def status(self, correlation_id: str) -> Tuple[str, Iterable[str]]: ...
invariants: Every forward step MUST declare a compensating action, or the saga CANNOT include it.
Compensation order SHALL be the reverse of the completed forward steps; out-of-order compensation is FORBIDDEN.
The orchestrator's state transitions MUST be persisted atomically with the command it emits so crashes NEVER leave dangling sagas.
A saga NEVER assumes strong consistency across services; all coordination SHALL be via asynchronous messages.
primitives.extension_contract: New business flows extend SagaOrchestrator by declaring a step definition and registering a handler and its compensator via a register decorator; cross-cutting concerns (timeouts, retries) plug in through middleware that MUST NOT alter the compensation order.

sources.locator: Chapter 4, Managing Transactions with Sagas, pp. 114-149

sources.source: Garcia-Molina and Salem 'Sagas' (1987) as cited in Richardson

primitives.why_essential: Without a shared primitive, cross-service flows degrade into ad-hoc scripts where partial failures leave the system in states no single tool can observe or recover from.
alternatives_considered: Distributed 2PC (XA): long locks, poor failure modes, not supported across HTTP services.
Pure choreography-only: simpler start but compensation logic gets duplicated per participant.
Ignore partial failure: silently corrupts cross-service state.

primitives.name: EventStream
primitives.purpose: An ordered, append-only log of events partitioned by key and replayable from any offset by any number of consumers.
primitives.api_signature:
from typing import Protocol, Any, Iterator

class EventStream(Protocol):
    def append(self, partition_key: str, event: Any) -> int: ...
    def read_from(self, partition_key: str, offset: int) -> Iterator[Any]: ...
    def tail(self, partition_key: str) -> int: ...
    def truncate_before(self, offset: int) -> None: ...
invariants: Events MUST be strictly ordered within a partition; cross-partition ordering is NEVER guaranteed.
Appended events CANNOT be mutated or deleted out of retention windows; immutability SHALL be enforced.
Consumers MUST be able to start from any valid offset and replay; destructive consumption is FORBIDDEN.
truncate_before ALWAYS obeys the configured retention policy; arbitrary backdated truncation is FORBIDDEN.
primitives.extension_contract: New transports extend EventStream by implementing the Protocol as an adapter over the underlying log and registering it with the stream registry; processing topologies compose via pluggable stages that MUST NOT break per-partition order.

sources.locator: Chapter 11, Partitioned Logs and stream processing, pp. 444-454
Chapter 3, Messaging and event logs, pp. 85-95

primitives.why_essential: Without a shared primitive, some tools emit point-in-time messages and others emit logs, making replay, debugging, and derived-view rebuilds impossible to compose.
alternatives_considered: Transient queues: cannot replay, so downstream rebuilds require ad-hoc backfill.
Database tables as queues: awkward partition semantics and poor consumer scaling.
File-based archives: lose online read semantics and partition keys.

primitives.name: EventSourcedStore
primitives.purpose: Persists aggregate state as an ordered sequence of domain events and reconstructs current state by folding them on load.
primitives.api_signature:
from typing import Protocol, Iterable, Any

class EventSourcedStore(Protocol):
    def load(self, aggregate_id: str) -> Iterable[Any]: ...
    def append(self, aggregate_id: str, expected_version: int, events: Iterable[Any]) -> int: ...
    def snapshot(self, aggregate_id: str, version: int, state: Any) -> None: ...
    def latest_snapshot(self, aggregate_id: str) -> Any: ...
invariants: append MUST fail with a concurrency error when expected_version does not match the current tail; last-writer-wins is FORBIDDEN.
Events already written CANNOT be mutated; corrections SHALL be expressed as new, compensating events.
Snapshots MUST be reproducible from the event log; the store NEVER treats a snapshot as the source of truth.
Replays from zero ALWAYS produce the same logical state given the same event sequence; non-determinism is FORBIDDEN.
primitives.extension_contract: New aggregate types extend EventSourcedStore by registering their event serializer and fold function via a register call on the store registry; storage backends plug in through an adapter without altering concurrency or replay semantics.

sources.locator: 'Event Sourcing' supplementary pattern (2005 essay building on PEAA terminology)
Appendix A, Aggregates and Event Sourcing, pp. 577-595

primitives.why_essential: Without a shared primitive, tools that adopt event sourcing drift in concurrency control, serialization, and snapshot policy, making one team's stream unreadable by another's replay.
alternatives_considered: State-based persistence only: loses audit, replay, and temporal queries.
Event log in a sidecar table with overwrites: gives the illusion of sourcing without the guarantees.
CRDT-based state: solves convergence but not intent tracking.

primitives.name: CommandQuerySeparator
primitives.purpose: Partitions the API into write commands that mutate state and read queries that observe it so each side can scale and evolve independently.
primitives.api_signature:
from typing import Protocol, Any

class CommandQuerySeparator(Protocol):
    def dispatch_command(self, command: Any) -> Any: ...
    def answer_query(self, query: Any) -> Any: ...
    def register_command_handler(self, command_type: type, handler) -> None: ...
    def register_query_handler(self, query_type: type, handler) -> None: ...
invariants: A command handler MUST NEVER return query results synthesized from the write model; it SHALL return only acknowledgement and identifiers.
A query handler CANNOT mutate state, invoke commands, or block on external side-effects.
Each command type MUST have at most one registered handler; duplicate handler registration is FORBIDDEN.
Read models ALWAYS receive updates through the same event stream as the write model; separate in-band write paths for reads are FORBIDDEN.
primitives.extension_contract: New operations extend CommandQuerySeparator by registering a command or query handler via a decorator and binding its schema to the API layer; cross-cutting policies (authz, logging) plug in through middleware that MUST respect the command/query split.
primitives.consumption_example:
def place(api: CommandQuerySeparator, cmd):
    ack = api.dispatch_command(cmd)
    view = api.answer_query({'order_id': cmd.order_id})
    return ack, view

Meyer's Command-Query Separation principle referenced, Chapter 9, pp. 147-149

primitives.why_essential: Without an enforced split, read-optimized shapes smear into write aggregates, denormalization leaks into the domain, and every team invents its own convention for 'which calls mutate'.
alternatives_considered: Single unified model: breaks at scale when read and write workloads diverge.
Conventional CRUD over ORM: entangles query projections with write invariants.
GraphQL resolvers without CQS: hides the mutation surface and complicates authorization.

cross_cutting_insights: Atomicity is the unifying concern: UnitOfWork, TransactionalOutbox, InboxDeduplicator, and EventSourcedStore all refuse the dual-write trap by co-locating a side-effect's record with the state change in one transaction.
Identity is explicit infrastructure: IdentityMap, Aggregate.id, DomainEvent.event_id, and EventStream partition keys each declare who or what a change belongs to so replay and dedupe remain sound.

Boundary discipline cascades: Evans's BoundedContext, Vernon's ContextMap, and the AntiCorruptionLayer together prevent the silent model drift that Richardson's saga and CQRS primitives assume is already handled.

Immutability is the cheap trick that unlocks replay: ValueObject, DomainEvent, and EventStream all forbid in-place mutation, which is precisely what makes MaterializedView rebuilds and EventSourcedStore folds deterministic.

At-least-once delivery is assumed end-to-end: TransactionalOutbox, IdempotentConsumer, InboxDeduplicator, and SagaOrchestrator all treat duplicates as the normal case and encode exactly-once as a property of the consumer, not the transport (Kleppmann Ch. 11).

Specification, Repository, and CommandQuerySeparator share one refactor path: they move policy out of callsites into a named object that tests, optimizers, and projections can all inspect without re-reading SQL strings.

CDC and Event Sourcing are rival origins for the same downstream primitives (MaterializedView, EventStream); the choice determines whether the log is derived from rows or whether rows are derived from the log, but the consumer contract stays identical.
gaps_observed: SKILL-001 lacks a first-class UnitOfWork primitive; commit boundaries are per-tool and leak across feature boundaries.
No TransactionalOutbox primitive exists; tools integrating with brokers rely on implicit dual writes.
IdempotentConsumer and InboxDeduplicator are not codified; each messaging consumer reinvents dedupe differently.
No ContextMap primitive is present; cross-module integration policy is tacit and undocumented.
MaterializedView and ChangeDataCapture are missing; cache and projection strategies vary by feature without a shared contract.
Specification is not a shared primitive; query criteria are inlined into repositories per tool.
SagaOrchestrator is absent; cross-service workflows are ad-hoc with no compensation registry.
EventSourcedStore is not offered as an option; aggregates cannot opt into sourcing without bespoke code.
CommandQuerySeparator is not enforced; read and write handlers intermix in most feature tools.
AntiCorruptionLayer has no primitive; third-party SDK types are imported directly into domain code.
